faq.a: No – continue to empty the breast; stopping increases stasis and worsens infection.
faq.q: Can I stop breastfeeding during mastitis?

faq.a: Generally avoid; they can introduce skin flora and delay healing.
faq.q: Is it safe to use herbal compresses on a sore nipple?

faq.a: When a collection >2 cm is seen or the breast does not improve after 48 h of antibiotics.

exam: What bedside signs differentiate acute mastitis from simple engorgement? — Look for fever, localized erythema, and systemic symptoms; engorgement lacks fever and has diffuse swelling.

A lactating mother presents with a painful, red breast and fever. Which empirical antibiotic would you choose and why? — Choose a penicillinase‑resistant anti‑staphylococcal drug (e.g., flucloxacillin) because MSSA is the common pathogen; it spares anaerobes and has low C. difficile risk.

How would you manage a 3‑cm fluctuant area in the upper outer quadrant after 24 h of antibiotics? — Arrange ultrasound if available; if abscess confirmed, perform incision and drainage while continuing antibiotics.
Why is it important to advise continued breastfeeding during treatment? — Ongoing milk removal prevents stasis, reduces bacterial load, and maintains lactation; cessation increases risk of abscess.
In an HIV‑positive mother with mastitis, what additional considerations are needed? — Be vigilant for atypical organisms, consider broader coverage, and monitor for rapid systemic spread.

What red‑flag features would prompt urgent referral to a higher‑level facility? — Sepsis signs (hypotension, tachypnea), large or rapidly expanding abscess, or failure to improve after 48 h of therapy.

How does inflammatory breast cancer mimic mastitis and how can you distinguish it? — Both cause redness and swelling, but cancer shows peau‑d’orange, persistent thickening, and no fever; lack of response to antibiotics is a clue.

If culture facilities are unavailable, how do you decide whether to change antibiotics? — Base decision on clinical response: worsening pain, persistent fever, or expanding swelling after 48 h warrants escalation.
ai.title: Acute Lactational Mastitis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Acute mastitis is a bacterial infection of breast tissue, usually occurring in the first weeks of lactation after nipple trauma. Prompt diagnosis, appropriate antibiotics and continued breastfeeding are key to prevent abscess and systemic spread.

b: Diagnosis is clinical; culture of expressed milk or pus confirms the pathogen.
Differential includes breast engorgement, cellulitis, inflammatory carcinoma.
sections.p: An acute inflammatory infection of the breast tissue occurring in lactating women, characterised by localized pain, erythema, swelling and systemic signs such as fever.

b: Mild: localized pain, <5 cm erythema, no systemic fever.
Moderate: >5 cm erythema, fever ≥38 °C, malaise.
Severe: signs of sepsis, rapidly expanding swelling, possible abscess formation.
sections.p: Severity is graded by extent of tissue involvement and systemic response.

b: Staphylococcus aureus (≈80 % of cases) – enters via cracked nipple.
Streptococcus pyogenes – more cellulitic pattern.
Mixed anaerobes – in women with poor drainage or prolonged stasis.
HIV infection – impairs local immunity, raises risk of atypical organisms.
Traditional herbal compresses – may introduce skin flora.
sections.p: In low‑resource settings the same organisms dominate, but co‑factors such as HIV, poor hygiene and traditional breast massage increase risk.

b: Unilateral breast pain, usually in the upper outer quadrant.
Erythema with a well‑demarcated border, sometimes with a “fluctuant” area.
Systemic fever ≥38 °C, tachycardia, malaise.
sections.p: The patient reports sudden breast pain, warmth and redness, often after a feeding session. Fever, chills and malaise develop within 24‑48 h.

t.b: Confirms localisation, assesses for fluctuance (abscess) – guides need for drainage.
Identifies pathogen and antibiotic susceptibility – essential if no improvement after 48 h.
Elevated white cell count (>12 × 10⁹/L) supports infection; if unavailable, rely on clinical fever.
Detects fluid collection >2 cm indicating abscess – indicates need for drainage.

b: Rapidly enlarging swelling, fluctuance → abscess.
Persistent fever >38 °C after 48 h of antibiotics → possible resistant organism.
Sepsis: hypotension, tachypnea, altered mental status.
Mastitis in HIV‑positive women may progress to necrotizing fasciitis.
sections.p: Complications arise when infection spreads or an abscess forms.

b: Empiric oral anti‑staphylococcal antibiotic (e.g., flucloxacillin) – covers MSSA; avoid clindamycin if high C. difficile risk.
If penicillin allergy, use a macrolide (e.g., erythromycin) – less effective against MRSA.
Continue breastfeeding or pumping to empty the breast; advise proper latch to prevent further trauma.
Analgesia with paracetamol; warm compresses before feeds.
If abscess >2 cm or not responding, arrange incision and drainage – can be done under local anaesthetic.
sections.p: Treat the infection, maintain milk flow and monitor for complications.

b: Check for resolution of pain, erythema and fever.
Teach proper hand hygiene, nipple care, and correct infant latch.
Consider prophylactic topical antiseptic (e.g., chlorhexidine) for women with recurrent cracks.
Screen HIV‑positive mothers for opportunistic breast infections.
sections.p: Re‑evaluate within 48 h; educate on techniques that reduce recurrence.

b: Breast engorgement – painful but no fever, resolves with frequent feeding.
Inflammatory breast cancer – peau‑d’orange, persistent thickening, no rapid fever.
Cellulitis of the chest wall – involves skin beyond breast margin.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic mastitis but require different management.

b: Normal white count does not exclude infection in early HIV or malnutrition.
Ultrasound may miss a small early abscess; clinical fluctuation remains gold standard.
sections.p: Laboratory and bedside findings may be deceptive in low‑resource settings.

whenToSeekHelp: High fever ≥39 °C, hypotension, or rapid deterioration.
Swelling that becomes hard, tender and fluctuates.
No improvement after 48 h of appropriate antibiotics.
